concept.body: A cross-section is the flat face where a plane slices a solid (Grade 7's definition, unchanged). Round-solid catalog: a cylinder gives circles (parallel to base), rectangles (parallel to axis), or ellipses (slant); a cone gives shrinking circles, a triangle through the apex, or ellipses; a sphere gives a circle for EVERY plane — largest through the center (the great circle), and off-center slices have radius √(R² − d²).

explanationVariants: Parallel to the base, a cylinder reprints its base.

widget.prompt: A cylinder of base radius 3 is sliced parallel to its base. The section is:

options.label: A circle of radius 3
options.feedback: Straight walls: every parallel slice copies the base.

options.label: A circle of radius 1.5
options.feedback: A cylinder never shrinks its slices — that's the cone's habit. Radius 3.

options.label: A rectangle
options.feedback: Rectangles come from axis-parallel cuts — base-parallel gives the circle.

options.label: An ellipse
options.feedback: Ellipses need slant — parallel keeps the perfect circle.

steps.body: Grade 7 sliced prisms and pyramids; now the round solids join. A **cross-section** is still the flat face where a plane slices a solid — and for a cylinder the catalog is tidy: slice **parallel to the base** and you get a circle congruent to it; slice **parallel to the axis** and you get a rectangle; slice at a slant and an ellipse appears.

explanationVariants: Parallel-to-base slices copy the base at every height.
A circle of the base's own radius, 4.

widget.prompt: A cylinder has base radius 4. A plane slices it parallel to the base, halfway up. The cross-section is:

options.label: A circle of radius 4 — congruent to the base at every height
options.feedback: The cylinder's walls rise straight, so every parallel slice reprints the base exactly — a fact Cavalieri's principle will soon lean on hard.

options.label: A circle smaller than the base
options.feedback: Shrinking slices belong to the CONE — a cylinder's parallel sections stay radius 4 the whole way up.

options.label: A rectangle
options.feedback: Rectangles come from slicing PARALLEL TO THE AXIS (through the standing direction) — parallel to the base gives the circle.

options.label: An ellipse
options.feedback: Ellipses need a SLANTED plane — parallel to the base keeps the circle.

explanationVariants: Parallel slices shrink as they approach the apex; a plane THROUGH the apex cuts along two slant lines.
Through the apex and the base: a triangle.

widget.prompt: A plane slices a cone straight down through its apex (and through the base). The cross-section is:

options.label: A triangle — two slant edges meeting at the apex over a diameter of the base
options.feedback: The apex cut exposes the cone's profile: an isosceles triangle whose equal sides are slant heights.

options.label: A circle
options.feedback: Circles come from slices PARALLEL to the base (smaller and smaller toward the apex) — the apex cut is a triangle.

options.label: An ellipse
options.feedback: Ellipses come from slanted planes that MISS the apex — through the apex, the section is a triangle.

options.label: A parabola opening sideways
options.feedback: Exotic sections exist for other cutting angles, but the through-the-apex vertical cut is the plain isosceles triangle.

steps.body: The sphere is the aristocrat: **every** planar slice of a sphere is a circle. Through the center, the slice is as large as possible — the **great circle**, radius equal to the sphere's own. Slice at distance d from the center and the disk's radius obeys chapter-friendly Pythagoras: r²ₛₗᵢᶜₑ = R² − d².

explanationVariants: The slice radius: √(5² − 3²) = √16 = 4 — a 3-4-5 inside the sphere.

widget.prompt: A sphere of radius 5 is sliced by a plane 3 units from its center. The cross-section's AREA (2 decimals, π ≈ 3.14159) = ?

commonErrors.feedback: 78.54 ≈ 25π is the GREAT circle's area — 3 units off-center, Pythagoras shrinks the radius to √(25 − 9) = 4: 16π ≈ 50.27.
12.57 ≈ 4π uses radius 2 — the slice radius is √(25 − 9) = 4, area 16π ≈ 50.27.
28.27 ≈ 9π squares the DISTANCE (3) — the slice radius is 4: 16π ≈ 50.27.

widget.fallbackFeedback: π(25 − 9) = 16π ≈ 50.27 — the same 3-4-5 disk the sphere-volume argument will slice next chapter.

predict.prompt: Slide a plane through a sphere. Where is the cross-section BIGGEST?

options.label: Exactly halfway — the slice through the centre
Near the top, where the surface curves hardest
Every parallel slice has the same area

predict.reveal: Halfway. Only the slice through the centre is a circle of the sphere's full radius; every other parallel cut is a smaller circle. Sweep the plane and watch the area readout rise to its maximum and fall away again.

widget.prompt: Sweep the section plane through the sphere and stop where the cross-sectional area is greatest.
widget.successFeedback: The middle slice wins: a circle of radius 5, area π(5²) ≈ 78.54 — the value the entry above asks for. It is the only cut that passes through the centre, so it is the only one that gets the whole radius.
widget.positionFeedback: Not the largest section yet — read the area as you move. It climbs toward the centre and falls away on either side.
widget.comparisonFeedback: Add the comparison solid to finish the reading.
widget.invariantFeedback: Try more heights first. One slice is a measurement; several slices are the evidence that the middle one is the maximum.

widget.prompt: A mystery solid: EVERY plane through it — any angle, any position — cuts a circle. The solid is:

options.label: A sphere — it's the only solid whose sections are circles in every direction
options.feedback: Cylinders and cones betray themselves with rectangles, triangles, or ellipses at other angles — all-circles-always is the sphere's signature.

options.label: A cylinder
options.feedback: Slice a cylinder along its axis: a rectangle. Only the sphere circles every plane.

options.label: A cone
options.feedback: Through the apex a cone shows a TRIANGLE — the all-circle solid is the sphere.

options.label: A cube with rounded corners
options.feedback: Its flat faces cut polygons — the sphere alone circles everything.

hints: The slice's radius comes from R² − d² — here the AREA is given, so run it backward.
36π = π r²ₛₗᵢᶜₑ gives the slice radius; then Pythagoras finds d.
explanationVariants: A 6-8-10 triangle inside the sphere: d = 8.

widget.prompt: A sphere of radius 10 is sliced by a plane, producing a cross-section of area 36π. How far is the plane from the sphere's center?

commonErrors.feedback: 6 is the SLICE's radius (√36) — the distance is the other leg: √(100 − 36) = 8.
64 is d², not d itself. Take the square root to finish: d = 8.
4 halves — 100 − 36 = 64, so d = 8 (the course's favorite 6-8-10 again).

takeaways: Cylinder: circle (parallel to base), rectangle (parallel to axis), ellipse (slant).
Cone: shrinking circles, apex-cut triangle, slant ellipses. Sphere: circles ALWAYS, greatest through the center.
Off-center sphere slices obey r²ₛₗᵢᶜₑ = R² − d² — Pythagoras inside the solid.
steps.teaser: Next: run slicing in reverse — spin a flat shape and SWEEP a solid.
